questions.prompt: What does “signal flow” describe?
choices: The path a signal takes through a system
How much reverb is on a signal
The kind of cable a signal travels on
questions.explanation: Signal flow is the path audio takes from its source through inputs, processing, routing, and outputs.

questions.prompt: A receiver shows microphone signal, but the mixer input meter shows nothing. What troubleshooting approach best follows signal flow?
choices: Check the cable and routing from the receiver to the mixer input
questions.explanation: Follow the signal in order. The receiver shows signal, so the mic is working; the problem is somewhere between the receiver output and the mixer input.

questions.prompt: A DAW is showing no microphone signal. Which should you check first?
choices: Whether the right input device and track input are selected
Whether the track is panned center
Whether the master fader is at 0 dB
Whether the track has EQ on it
questions.explanation: Correct I/O is fundamental: the DAW must use the intended device and the track must listen to the correct input.

questions.prompt: You want to record through an audio interface, but the DAW is still using the computer’s built-in microphone. What needs to change?
questions.explanation: The DAW records from whichever input device is selected in its audio settings. Choose the interface there, then pick the right input on the track.

questions.prompt: Before recording into a DAW track, what usually needs to be enabled on that track?
questions.explanation: Record-arming tells the DAW which track should receive and record the incoming signal.

questions.prompt: You press Record and the playhead moves, but no new audio appears on your microphone track. What is a likely cause?
choices: The master fader is at 0 dB
questions.explanation: Only record-armed tracks capture new audio. If the track isn’t armed, the DAW runs without recording onto it.

questions.prompt: Which control should you use first to get a healthy microphone level entering a mixer or interface?
questions.explanation: Input gain sets the level entering the channel. Faders are normally used afterward to balance signals in a mix.

questions.prompt: A microphone is extremely quiet at the channel input. Which control is the most direct first adjustment?
questions.explanation: Input gain sets how strongly the mic signal enters the channel. Faders come later, for balancing a signal that’s already healthy.

questions.prompt: In a digital recording system, what is the main problem with reaching or exceeding 0 dBFS?
questions.explanation: 0 dBFS is the digital ceiling. Trying to go beyond it causes clipping.

questions.prompt: Your input meter hits the red clip light during the loudest passages. What should you do before the real take?
choices: Turn down the input gain and test again
Turn down only the main fader
questions.explanation: The clipping is happening at the input, so lower the input gain. Turning down a fader later won’t remove distortion that was already recorded.

questions.prompt: What is the simplest difference between mono and stereo audio?
choices: Mono uses one channel; stereo uses two channels
Mono is quiet; stereo is loud
Mono is analog; stereo is digital
Mono uses XLR; stereo uses USB
questions.explanation: Mono is one channel. Stereo uses two channels, normally left and right.

questions.prompt: You are recording one microphone into Input 1. What track format is usually appropriate?
questions.explanation: One microphone feeding one interface input is a mono source, so a mono DAW track is normally appropriate.

questions.prompt: Which microphone type commonly requires 48V phantom power?
questions.explanation: Condenser microphones commonly need phantom power. Dynamic microphones generally do not.

questions.prompt: You connect a condenser microphone and the input meter shows nothing. Which setting is worth checking first?
questions.explanation: Many condenser microphones require 48V phantom power to operate.

questions.prompt: What is a basic job of an audio interface?
choices: Connect mics and instruments to the computer, and send audio back out
Automatically mix and master a song
Replace the need for a DAW
questions.explanation: An audio interface connects analog audio sources and outputs with the computer and commonly contains preamps and converters.

questions.prompt: When you record into a computer through an audio interface, where does the microphone plug in?
choices: An XLR/combo input on the interface
questions.explanation: Microphones connect to the interface’s inputs, usually XLR/combo jacks. The interface’s preamp and converter then send the signal to the computer.

questions.prompt: A recording call begins at 7:00 p.m. What best matches the course idea of being “on time”?
choices: Send a message at 7:05 saying you are parking
questions.explanation: For recording work, being on time means being ready to work at the scheduled time, not merely arriving at that moment.

questions.prompt: A problem will make you late for a recording call. What best matches the course professionalism standard?
choices: Wait until after the recording to mention it
Only tell another student after the start time
questions.explanation: Reliability includes communicating early, before a scheduling problem becomes a larger problem.

questions.prompt: Your group finishes a camera activity. What best matches “finish the job”?
choices: Restore default settings and return the gear and batteries
Leave as soon as your clips are recorded
Leave the camera on so the next group is ready
Keep the SD card in your bag to check later
questions.explanation: The job isn’t done until the gear is reset and returned. The next person should find it ready to use, with batteries back where they belong.

questions.prompt: Who is the monitor mix mainly for?
questions.explanation: Monitors help performers hear themselves. Their mix can be different from the audience’s Main L/R mix.

questions.prompt: Why might a monitor mix be different from the mains?
choices: Performers may need different things emphasized than the audience does
questions.explanation: Performers often need a custom balance so they can hear what helps them perform, while mains are mixed for the audience.

questions.prompt: A singer asks for more of their own voice on stage without making it louder for the audience. What should you adjust?
questions.explanation: The monitor mix is for the performer and can be adjusted independently from the audience mix.

questions.prompt: What is the basic difference between an active speaker and a passive speaker?
choices: An active speaker has amplification built in; a passive speaker needs an external amplifier
Active speakers use XLR; passive speakers use USB
questions.explanation: Active/powered speakers contain an amplifier. Passive speakers need an external power amplifier.

questions.prompt: You’re setting up a passive speaker. What does it need between the mixer and the speaker?
questions.explanation: A passive speaker has no amplifier inside, so the mixer’s output has to go through a power amplifier first.

questions.prompt: What is the safe basic power rule for speakers?
choices: Speakers ON last and OFF first
Speakers ON first and OFF last
Speakers must stay on all day
questions.explanation: Turning speakers on last and off first helps prevent loud pops and surprises from upstream equipment.

questions.prompt: You are shutting down a live sound system. Which should happen first?
choices: Turn off every microphone before anything else
questions.explanation: Speakers and amplifiers should be turned off first during shutdown to reduce the chance of loud pops.

questions.prompt: What is feedback in a live sound system?
choices: Sound from a speaker re-enters a microphone and loops through the system
A DAW exports a WAV file
A passive speaker receives amplifier power
questions.explanation: Feedback occurs when amplified sound returns to a microphone and is amplified again in a loop.

questions.prompt: A vocal mic starts to squeal whenever the singer walks in front of the main speakers. What’s the best first fix?
choices: Keep the mic behind the speakers and pointed away from them
Turn up the mic’s input gain
questions.explanation: Feedback happens when the speakers’ sound gets back into the mic. Keeping mics behind the speakers and aimed away from them breaks the loop.

questions.prompt: Aperture/iris is primarily a control related to what?
choices: How much light enters through the lens
questions.explanation: Aperture/iris changes the lens opening and therefore affects how much light reaches the camera sensor.

questions.prompt: You change the aperture from F4 to F5.6. What happens?
choices: Less light gets in, because the opening is smaller
More light gets in, because the opening is bigger
questions.explanation: A higher f-number means a smaller lens opening, so F5.6 lets in less light than F4.

questions.prompt: Shutter speed is part of which general camera task?
questions.explanation: Shutter speed affects exposure and also changes how motion is rendered.

questions.prompt: What happens to moving subjects when you use a much slower shutter speed?
choices: They look sharper and more frozen
questions.explanation: A slower shutter exposes each frame for longer, so movement smears into motion blur. The image also gets brighter.

questions.prompt: What is the usual tradeoff when you raise a camera’s gain/ISO?
choices: The image gets brighter but noisier (grainier)
The image gets darker but sharper
questions.explanation: Gain/ISO brightens the image electronically, and that adds visible noise, or grain.

questions.prompt: White balance is mainly used to control what?
questions.explanation: White balance tells the camera how to interpret color under different lighting. Kelvin is commonly used to set color temperature.

questions.prompt: A shot looks unnaturally blue or orange under the room lighting. Which setting is most directly related?
questions.explanation: White balance controls how the camera interprets color under the current lighting.

questions.prompt: What is the simplest purpose of focus?
choices: Make the intended subject appear sharp
questions.explanation: Focus determines what distance/subject appears sharp in the image.

questions.prompt: Which stereo technique uses two directional microphones with capsules very close together and angled apart?
questions.explanation: XY is a coincident stereo technique: the microphone capsules are placed very close together and angled apart.

questions.prompt: Why does an XY recording usually hold up well when it’s summed to mono?
choices: The capsules are nearly in the same spot, so sound reaches both at the same time
questions.explanation: With the capsules together there’s almost no time difference between the two mics, so combining them avoids the phase cancellation a spaced pair can have.

questions.prompt: Which technique is commonly described as a spaced pair of microphones?
questions.explanation: A/B uses two microphones spaced apart to capture stereo information.

questions.prompt: ORTF is best described as which kind of setup?
questions.explanation: ORTF is a near-coincident stereo technique: two cardioid microphones about 17 cm apart, angled 110° from each other.

questions.prompt: In the current basic stereo-recording activity, how should the two microphone input gains generally be treated?
choices: Set to matching values unless there is a specific reason not to
One must always be at minimum
The right side must always be louder
questions.explanation: The activity calls for matching gains so the stereo pair begins from a balanced setup.

questions.prompt: For a basic two-channel stereo recording, how are the channels normally panned?
questions.explanation: A basic stereo pair needs distinct left and right channels so the spatial information is preserved.

questions.prompt: Both stereo mic tracks recorded cleanly, but playback sounds like everything is in the middle. What’s the likely setup mistake?
choices: The input gain is too high
questions.explanation: With both channels panned center, the left/right differences collapse into the middle. Pan one hard left and the other hard right.

questions.prompt: In the X32 activity, buses are used for what important task?
questions.explanation: Buses can create separate mixes, such as Monitor 1 and Monitor 2, that differ from the Main L/R mix.

questions.prompt: What does Sends on Fader help you adjust on the X32?
choices: How much of each input is sent to a selected bus
questions.explanation: Sends on Fader lets the faders represent channel send levels into the selected bus, which is useful for monitor mixes.

questions.prompt: What is Dante Controller mainly used for in these activities?
choices: Routing network audio transmitters to receivers
questions.explanation: Dante Controller provides the routing matrix used to connect Dante transmit and receive channels.

questions.prompt: What role does Dante Virtual Soundcard (DVS) play?
choices: It lets a computer send/receive audio channels on the Dante network
questions.explanation: DVS allows computer audio software to use Dante network channels as audio I/O.

questions.prompt: In a Dante routing matrix, what are you creating when you click the intersection between a transmitter channel and receiver channel?
questions.explanation: The matrix intersection connects a transmitting Dante channel to a receiving Dante channel.

questions.prompt: In Dante, what does a transmitter channel do?
questions.explanation: Transmitters send audio onto the Dante network and receivers pick it up. The routing matrix connects a transmitter channel to a receiver channel.

questions.prompt: Why is signal-flow thinking especially useful in a live-looping rig?
choices: Several devices and effects must be connected in the correct order
questions.explanation: A live-looping setup may pass through instruments, effects, a looper, vocal processing, and speakers, so following the signal path is essential.
